new_statements.quote: These distinctions not only reflect vowel length but also affect the stress patterns, since primary word stress normally falls on the penultimate vowel and secondary stress on the one or more preceding vowels. By contrast, utterance stress creates a succession of alternated stressed and unstressed vowels. [Minimal pairs on the same page: a aˈro:ha ‘compassion’ / aroˈha: ‘underside of chin’; o ˈmano ‘ten thousand’ / maˈno: ‘shark’; u ˈtaku ‘my’ / taˈku: ‘adze’.]
new_statements.citation: Moyle, Richard M. 2011. Takuu grammar and dictionary: a Polynesian language of the South Pacific (Pacific Linguistics 634). Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 'Brief grammatical sketch', section 2.1 Phonology, p. 7 (PDF page 18 of the ANU repository file); stress-marked minimal pairs on the same page; question intonation p. 23 (PDF p. 34)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (439 PDF pages, text layer present; re-extracted PDF pp. 18-19 and 34 with extracted text, no scanned). QUOTE: on PDF p. 18 = printed p. 7 (running head 'Brief grammatical sketch 7', section 2.1 Phonology, directly under the vowel-length minimal pairs) the passage is there word for word: 'These distinctions not only reflect vowel length but also affect the stress patterns, since primary word stress normally falls on the penultimate vowel and secondary stress on the one or more preceding vowels. By contrast, utterance stress creates a succession of alternated stressed and unstressed vowels.' The minimal pairs on the same page are exactly as reported (aˈro:ha 'compassion' / aroˈh…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate vowel counted by morae: a long vowel counts as two (p. 7 'a long vowel counts as two mora'), so a word-final long vowel takes the stress (taˈku: 'adze' vs ˈtaku 'my'; maˈno: 'shark' vs ˈmano). Equivalent to 'stress the penultimate mora', i.e. a quantity-sensitive right-edge rule of the usual Polynesian type; vowel-length contrasts thus shift the stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on 'the one or more preceding vowels' (no explicit alternation rule for the word; at utterance level 'a succession of alternated stressed and unstressed vowels').
new_statements.exceptions: 'normally' — no lexical exceptions listed. One- and two-syllable words are not cited in isolation: a minimal utterance needs four morae (verbs prefixed by lengthened e:, nouns take an article) (p. 7). Utterance-level stress overrides word stress. Polar questions are marked by rising pitch on the penultimate syllable and falling pitch on the final; if the final syllable is a long vowel the fall is realised on that syllable alone (p. 23).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('primary word stress'), explicitly contrasted with utterance stress. Moyle's fn. 1 (p. 7) says the phonology discussion 'draw[s] substantially on' Clark 1998 (Mele) and Donner 1987 (Sikaiana); the stress sentence is near-verbatim Donner's Sikaiana wording, but the stress-marked Takuu minimal pairs are Moyle's own data and confirm the mora-counting penult rule for Takuu.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Takuu proper (Takū/Mortlock atoll, Bougainville, PNG), i.e. taku1257 itself; no dialects distinguished. Note the provenance caveat: Moyle's stress sentence is modelled on Donner 1987 (Sikaiana, sika1261, already in our catalog with near-identical wording) per his own footnote, so the two catalog entries are not fully independent in wording, though the Takuu minimal pairs (ˈtaku vs taˈku:) are first-hand Takuu data.
